World, process, and expression

Borrow Fire, Then Become Fire · MAIN SEQUENCE 06 / 18

Understanding: finite inquiry in a changing world

Distinguish world, process, model, and expression so representations guide action and meet correction.

完整中文版

A frame catches a crossing of the current. It leaves the water outside its edges, yet someone who sees the frame notices a path they had not seen before. The image returns to the river as a new way of looking.

Yinyang models human and model activity as interacting event streams. This essay develops what that common form makes distinguishable: the process being understood, a model of it, an expression carrying the model, and the world in which an expression has consequences. Their connections make inquiry possible; their differences make correction possible. Its computational ontology develops usable relations through which an encounter becomes intelligible and its consequences become available for further inquiry.

Here ontology means an articulation of the objects, roles, relations, and transformations an inquiry needs. Computational emphasizes that these distinctions can be organized, transformed, and used in reasoning and action. Yinyang names the contemporary framework in which a person and a generative model contribute to each other's continuing activity. Their models of the person, the counterpart's role, and their relationship guide how they organize the environment. That environment includes Skills, prompts, hooks, tools, model choices, and the user's working conditions: the concrete arrangements through which an understanding acquires effects. The question is how expressions mediate this passage from understanding to action and back.

Physical ground and computational abstraction

This framework takes a physical world as its common ground. Thinking, feeling, model inference, writing, and making are activities within that world. Its computational ontology is an upper-level abstraction of physical processes: it selects events, states, relations, constraints, and transformations through which a particular question can be understood and worked on. The whole account of knowing, valuing, methods, and practice operates at these abstracted levels.

A physical basis alone does not supply a usable calculation. To answer a question, an inquirer still needs relevant variables, a scale, bridge assumptions, and a method that can operate within available resources. Reconstructing every microphysical detail of a conversation would not itself specify what counts as a correction or which consequence answers its question. Abstraction makes such relations available while physical conditions constrain their realization.

The same activity can therefore have a physical description and a computational, psychological, or practical description. Their relation must be investigated where the question needs it; a shared physical basis does not establish a complete reduction or make every higher-level problem tractable. The layers diagram shows this relationship, and Trinity develops its philosophical unity.

A process exceeds its available model

A stream is organized continuation, not merely a chronological transcript. Perception, interpretation, remembering, expression, and action can overlap, depend on earlier occurrences, or become explicit at different times. An available record captures some of those relations; other activity may never have been recorded. A local model makes selected objects, roles, dependencies, and transformations available for a particular inquiry. It does not contain the entire process that generated it.

Distinguish that model from its expression. A sentence, diagram, paper, or program gives a relation a form that can be encountered. Producing and reading the expression are themselves events in the continuing process. A model can have several expressions, and one expression can admit competing readings. Its occurrence, interpreted meaning, inferential consequences, and adequacy to its subject are different questions. Later understanding may reorganize what an earlier expression means without changing its original occurrence.

Fiction makes this difference especially visible: constructing and encountering a fictional work can have actual consequences without its characters existing as described. A literary image can gather possibilities before one interpretation is selected. Neither construction nor consequence makes every assertion drawn from that image true.

Screenshot and front end

A screenshot selects a moment and a frame from an activity that continues beyond it. A front end makes some of that activity perceptible and available for participation. As images of expression, they pose different questions: what has been selected, and what can a reader or participant now do through that selection? A diagram, prototype, or paragraph can show a relation without displaying every occurrence that produced it.

Selection is both the expression's strength and a possible source of error. An account that displayed everything without distinction might fail to make anything intelligible. Yet a clear arrangement can conceal an uncertainty that would change the next judgment. An adequate expression therefore needs fidelity to what matters for its use, rather than an impossible duplication of the whole process. The question is which relations, assumptions, and unresolved alternatives must remain visible.

This also changes how collaboration can be organized. A model can carry retrieval, construction, and verification while a person understands, selects, and corrects through what becomes visible. Both can contribute to either side of that arrangement. An expression mediates participation: what it makes perceptible can change what happens next. A prototype can let the person recognize a relation through use, while an explanation lets either participant inspect why the prototype behaves as it does. Visibility and execution support each other, and their allocation can change with the work.

Question-relative objects meet resistance

A question may make a person, utterance, memory, hypothesis, relationship, or work its object. That choice determines which distinctions the inquiry needs; it does not determine whether the answer is correct. The object can resist its description through an omitted relation, an unexpected result, or a failed prediction. Such resistance can require another abstraction, not merely another answer within the existing one.

Question-relative ontology therefore allows construction without treating reality as an arbitrary product of naming. Stable objects, recurring patterns, and scientific laws can remain supported across changing descriptions. The person also exceeds a self-description: continuity may involve bodily life, memory, relationships, commitments, and action without requiring an invariant explicit account of oneself.

Revisability follows from incomplete access, changing questions, and the demand to answer to evidence. A stable distinction can remain useful through many changes because it continues to describe the relations that matter. Checking its applicability connects that stability with the continuing process. Retaining a source, entertaining a candidate, and accepting a claim remain different acts, as developed in reasoning within an unfinished stream.

Physical realization and functional likeness

Human inquiry occurs under bodily, social, and material conditions. Model use depends on implemented computation, data, infrastructure, and interaction. Those conditions matter to what can be perceived, retained, expressed, and done. A realization claim connects a function to a particular mechanism and needs evidence at that level. Similar roles or observable performances do not establish identical human and model architectures, mechanisms, or experiences.

Computational articulation follows the relations needed to explain and act: what an occurrence changes, how retention informs a judgment, and which consequences distinguish candidate interpretations. A microphysical explanation asks how such activity is realized; ultimate reduction asks whether the higher-level account can be derived from a proposed basis. Those further questions require their own bridge assumptions and evidence. The functional account has an immediate use in comparing interpretations and organizing work; finite inquiry and abstraction develops its relation to physical reduction.

Three material and epistemic relations should also remain distinct:

Question Relation being investigated
Where did the materials come from? A history of formation and transformation.
What supplies energy to the activity now? Its current operating conditions and energy transfers.
What does the activity express, and is the claim supported? Information, interpretation, inference, and evidence.

The Department of Energy describes natural photosynthesis and research on converting sunlight into chemical fuels. This gives sunlight a concrete relation to chemical energy: incoming radiation can be transformed into stored energy available for later activity. DOE, “Solar Fuels”.

NASA describes the Sun and planets forming from a common collapsing cloud and protoplanetary disk. That is a material history, distinct from present-day sunlight powering an activity. A manufactured semiconductor has a history of material extraction and fabrication; a computing installation has its own present energy supply. Tracing those relations calls for evidence about the particular material and installation. NASA, “How did our Solar System form?”.

These distinctions are this essay's inference from the different questions. Material history explains where a medium came from; energy transfer explains how activity is sustained; interpretation and evidence explain what an expression warrants. Assessing an output connects its production with the particular claim and object it is meant to address.

A work returns to the encounter

A work acquires relative independence from the encounter that produced it. A paper can be challenged, a program can run differently from its author's expectation, and an image can be understood differently by another reader. Reception, operation, and resistance provide evidence neither participant can settle by preference alone. The work can change subsequent understanding and action while retaining its provenance.

In the Sun–Moon–Earth relation, Earth names the environment where these consequences occur. Roles do not fix either participant's faculties: both can generate, interpret, judge, and revise. Return can revise the account of the person, the counterpart, or their relationship, as well as the work itself. These revisions can overlap: trying a tool can change the understanding of a role while a new reading changes the tool's purpose. A new question can emerge from reception, and a useful stable arrangement can survive it.

An unfinished relation becomes a sentence. On the page it can answer back: its implication was not the one its author expected. Returning to it, the author sees an earlier thought differently and can begin from somewhere new.

This return has at least two distinguishable effects. An expression's meaning can be reorganized in the present, and its maker's understanding of what they were doing can change. The original occurrence retains its history. A later reading does not rewrite it; it establishes another relation to it. The distance between author and work is productive because the work can be encountered by others and by the author as a reader, rather than remaining identical to an intention.

In model-supported work, a partial intuition may become an argument or prototype. Reading it can disclose what fits, what is missing, or what the person did not mean. Revision participates in finding the relation being expressed. This can change a capacity to understand and generate as well as the artifact. The developmental question is what the person can now recognize, express, or do differently. A clearer artifact and a changed capacity are related outcomes whose connection becomes visible through subsequent participation.

Hegelian comparison and its limits

Hegel's Philosophy of Spirit places absolute spirit in relation to subjective and objective spirit and develops art, religion, and philosophy within its account. These categories articulate forms through which spirit develops consciousness, freedom, and self-knowledge. Hegel, §§553 onward.

Subjective spirit includes the development of consciousness and theoretical and practical activity. Hegel, Subjective Spirit. The objective dimension concerns freedom taking public and institutional form, including law and ethical life. Absolute spirit develops artistic, religious, and philosophical forms of self-comprehension within that system. These relations give externalization its philosophical significance: its meaning depends on the form of life and understanding in which it participates.

His Introduction to the Philosophy of History connects self-knowledge and freedom with public life and world history. Its object is wider than a person's local account of inquiry. The comparison here takes up one relation within that wider problem: how an expression gains distance and returns to self-understanding. Yinyang develops this relation at the scale of a person's encounter with generative intelligence, where a work becomes an object through which its maker can recognize and revise their activity. Hegel, Introduction. The linked texts provide the public sources for this bounded comparison.

Aesthetics participates in discovery

Light, color, spatial arrangement, parallel expression, condensation, and a second reflective voice can make relations perceptible. Bilingual articulation can expose differences between conceptual vocabularies. Such organization can participate in finding a relation, rather than merely decorating an already completed argument. A work's sensible form can reveal what a previous formulation kept distant or difficult to compare.

Condensation can keep several possibilities available long enough to compare them. Their differences can then be unfolded into premises, explanations, or practical choices. Aesthetic form helps relations become perceptible; definition and proof establish inferential connections; evidence tests claims about the world. Their contributions meet in a work while supporting different claims. The Sun–Moon–Earth image and the miniature maker give these relations other expressive forms. Their interpretation and realization remain open to the world's answer.

Source and claim scope

The linked public sources support their bounded scientific and philosophical claims; the distinctions connecting them are Yinyang's contemporary argument. The essay develops the objects needed to ask more precise questions and to let their answers change the account.
